title: Language translation using PHP
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content:
When attempting to translate a PHP application into languages like Persian (Farsi), running into issues that work for German but fail for others usually points to a misunderstanding of how text directionality interacts with HTML structure and character encoding, rather than a flaw in the translation logic itself. The code snippet provided demonstrates a basic string replacement mechanism using a `Translator` class that loads key-value pairs from a file. While the logic for swapping strings is sound, applying it to Persian requires specific handling of Right-to-Left (RTL) text flow and proper Unicode encoding support, which are often overlooked in simple implementations.

The primary technical hurdle with Persian translation is the character set. The provided code uses `ISO-8859-15` (Latin-1), an encoding designed exclusively for Western European languages. This charset does not contain characters from the Arabic script used in Farsi. If you attempt to load a `.txt` file containing Persian text or render it with this encoding, the browser will display garbled characters or question marks because the byte sequences do not map to valid glyphs. You must switch the meta tag in your HTML head to `UTF-8`. This ensures that every character from the Farsi script is interpreted correctly by the browser and the PHP engine.

Beyond encoding, the layout of your HTML needs to adapt to Right-to-Left text flow. German is Left-to-Right (LTR), so a form element appears normally. Persian requires the entire document or at least the content blocks to be mirrored. You cannot rely solely on changing the language parameter; you must inject CSS rules that set `direction: rtl` and `text-align: right` for the body or specific containers when the Farsi locale is active. Without these styles, the text will appear backwards, and logical elements like form labels might end up in visually incorrect positions relative to their inputs.

To implement this robustly without switching frameworks immediately, consider creating a configuration array within your `Translator` class that holds CSS directives per language. When initializing the translator with `'fa'`, you can output a `<style>` block or dynamically modify the document direction. This keeps the separation of concerns clean: the translation logic handles string replacement, while a helper function manages the layout shift required for RTL languages.

If your project scope expands beyond simple string interpolation, relying on static text files becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. Manual management of thousands of keys across multiple languages is error-prone and slows down development cycles. In scenarios where you require scalable internationalization with built-in support for complex layouts like Persian, leveraging a dedicated framework ecosystem is often the pragmatic choice. Laravel, for instance, provides robust localization helpers that abstract away the file loading and encoding concerns. You can find more details on how to handle such multilingual architectures at https://laravelcompany.com.

Finally, always ensure your translation files are saved with UTF-8 BOM removed or explicitly without BOM to prevent issues in some PHP environments, though modern servers generally handle UTF-8 natively. By combining the correct character encoding, explicit RTL CSS styling, and a scalable approach to managing translations, you can successfully deploy a Persian version of your site that feels native to Farsi users rather than just a mirrored German interface.
